frictionVectors.title: EU Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains reliant on Algerian gas, but pricing, contract terms, and decarbonization could reduce Algiers' leverage over time. Algeria is using its energy position to preserve strategic autonomy rather than accepting external policy alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Investment Constraints
frictionVectors.details: State dominance and regulatory restrictions limit technology and capital inflows outside hydrocarbons. Chinese infrastructure and Russian defense ties provide alternatives but can deepen dependence in selected sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure-for-finance arrangements and oil-backed obligations have reduced fiscal flexibility, even as Angola seeks to renegotiate and diversify creditors. Chinese firms remain important across construction, logistics, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and high operating costs threaten production growth, leaving the state vulnerable to foreign operators, service companies, and volatile prices. New investment is needed to preserve national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from Burkina Faso and Niger is pressuring northern Benin and increasing dependence on foreign security assistance. Attacks threaten transport corridors, border communities, and the state's ability to control frontier resources.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with neighboring military governments can disrupt customs flows through the Port of Cotonou and raise the cost of securing regional commerce. Benin is strengthening port infrastructure while trying to avoid overreliance on any single external partner.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured greater value capture from its diamond partnership, but the relationship remains exposed to global demand weakness and corporate restructuring. Maintaining local sorting, marketing, and beneficiation capacity is central to sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Risk
frictionVectors.details: New copper, nickel, and battery-mineral projects could reduce diamond dependence but may create fresh exposure to foreign capital and offtake agreements. The government's challenge is to attract investment without surrendering excessive fiscal or processing leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Reassertion
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over industrial mining, local processing, and gold marketing, while reducing the role of Western operators. This may increase domestic capture but risks deterring investment and shifting trade into opaque channels.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cooperation with Russian-linked security actors offers an alternative to France and other Western partners but creates new political and operational dependencies. Persistent jihadist attacks continue to restrict access to mines, roads, and rural production zones.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mineral exports
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal gold and 3TG minerals remain vulnerable to informal cross-border flows and weak state oversight. Prospective nickel development could deepen reliance on foreign capital without stronger licensing transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Tanzania-Rwanda corridor exposure
frictionVectors.details: Burundi depends heavily on neighboring states and Tanzanian routes for fuel, imports, and mineral exports. Periodic tension with Rwanda increases the political risk surrounding alternative trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External control of connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, tourism, and digital infrastructure depend substantially on foreign investors and development partners. This supports growth but limits domestic leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime-security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde relies on international cooperation to police its large Atlantic maritime zone against illegal fishing and narcotics trafficking. Security partnerships can constrain autonomous control of maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-financed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port, rail, and road projects have improved export capacity while increasing reliance on external contractors, lenders, and operating expertise. The Kribi corridor is strategically valuable but not fully controlled domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, gas, and timber concessions
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon, mining, and logging projects remain dominated by foreign firms and politically connected intermediaries. Weak transparency and conflict-affected regions reduce the state's ability to capture broad public value.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security influence
frictionVectors.details: Bangui's dependence on Russian-linked security forces has expanded Moscow's political and commercial access. Gold and diamond concessions remain central to concerns that security assistance is exchanged for opaque resource privileges.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese mining expansion
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked operators are active in gold and other extractive sectors, often amid weak regulatory capacity and local disputes. Poor transport links and insecurity make concession holders more influential than state institutions in producing areas.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and operator dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's oil exports depend on the cross-border pipeline through Cameroon and on foreign technical and financial partners. Disputes over operator ownership, taxation, and revenue control expose the limits of national sovereignty over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan war spillover
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan is driving refugees, arms flows, and armed-group activity toward Chad's eastern border. The crisis increases reliance on external security and humanitarian support while diverting attention from domestic resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: French Territorial Leverage
frictionVectors.details: France retains decisive influence through Mayotte, migration controls, aid, and security ties, while Moroni continues to contest the island's status. The dispute limits Comoros' diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Ports and Energy
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic capital leaves transport, telecommunications, and energy infrastructure reliant on foreign partners and financing. Gulf, French, and other external actors compete for influence without yet establishing exclusive control.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Linked Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to threaten mining areas in the east, weakening state control over gold, tantalum, tin, and related trade routes. Regional accusations and foreign commercial demand compound the sovereignty problem.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contracts and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms remain central to large-scale mining and infrastructure arrangements, while Kinshasa seeks greater local processing, revenue transparency, and renegotiation leverage. Financing needs constrain the government's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export capacity remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving national resource control exposed to production cycles, foreign operators, and opaque revenue governance. Diversification has progressed slowly.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and creditor relationships provide essential roads, ports, and public works but increase dependence on external capital. Debt servicing and contract transparency remain persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Export Chains
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain influential in cocoa, mining, energy, and logistics, limiting domestic value capture despite stronger regulation and local-processing ambitions. Commodity-price exposure continues to constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal and Sahel Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and northern corridors face spillover risks from Sahel instability and transnational smuggling. Côte d'Ivoire is expanding security and regional infrastructure cooperation to protect trade sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its strategic position through US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, gaining revenue and security guarantees while accepting unusually dense external influence over sovereign space.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: China-linked port, rail, and logistics projects are central to the economy but have increased exposure to debt, refinancing pressure, and strategic creditor leverage. Competition among external powers gives Djibouti bargaining power but narrows independent policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and asset monetization
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and Gulf investment are expanding foreign influence over strategic assets and infrastructure. Debt-service pressures constrain Cairo's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and canal security
frictionVectors.details: Regional attacks and instability threaten Suez Canal revenues and maritime security. Egypt must balance cooperation with Gulf states, Western navies, and neighboring powers.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing hydrocarbon assets
frictionVectors.details: Declining production increases dependence on foreign operators, technical partners, and external capital. The state retains formal control but faces weaker bargaining power as fields mature.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Large public works and energy projects remain vulnerable to contractor, lender, and procurement dependence. China and other external partners retain significant influence over implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects rely heavily on foreign companies and technology, limiting domestic value capture. Revenue transparency and sanctions risk complicate long-term resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline gives it strategic leverage amid conflicts around the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. External security competition creates opportunities for bargaining but also raises sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South Africa for trade routes, energy, finance, and market access. This limits independent control over strategic infrastructure and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and trade-preference exposure
frictionVectors.details: The sugar economy remains sensitive to European and regional trade rules, while manufacturing depends on external incentives and imported inputs. Policy autonomy is constrained by the need to preserve preferential access.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and GERD diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam increases Ethiopia's control over domestic power generation and regional water diplomacy. Disputes with Egypt and Sudan remain a persistent security risk.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages increase reliance on international lenders and external partners. Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing all shape the terms of infrastructure and resource development.

highlights: Junta Converts Power Into Resource Leverage
Manganese and Oil Contracts Under Review

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Concession Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in oil, manganese, and timber, creating friction with established French, Chinese, and other foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon’s resource exports remain dependent on aging rail and port infrastructure, limiting bargaining power despite efforts to diversify external investors.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional trade, transport, and security, giving Dakar substantial influence over Banjul’s economic and infrastructure choices.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries Access Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing pressure and weak monitoring capacity continue to reduce local control over marine resources and generate tensions with coastal communities.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Gold Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey damages water systems and agricultural land while weakening formal state oversight, with foreign financiers and trading networks benefiting from opaque gold flows.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Accra is trying to secure more domestic value from lithium, bauxite, and gold, but IMF-linked fiscal constraints and competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors limit negotiating flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Enclave Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led bauxite and iron-ore projects generate export revenue but leave Guinea exposed to concession asymmetries, limited local processing, and weak transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Infrastructure Control
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and mining infrastructure around Simandou will determine whether the state captures broad developmental gains or remains dependent on multinational operators and external lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Processing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and public finances vulnerable to foreign buyers, price swings, and port bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Narco-Political and Port Risks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political instability enable illicit trafficking networks to exploit maritime and airport infrastructure, undermining state control and external investor confidence.

highlights: Regional logistics hub retains strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt-servicing pressure keeps Nairobi reliant on IMF support and external creditors, narrowing room for independent fiscal and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing Chinese-linked infrastructure exposure with Gulf and Western investment around Mombasa, Lamu, and regional transport corridors.

highlights: Water sovereignty tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho’s revenues and infrastructure prospects remain closely tied to water transfers to South Africa, giving Pretoria substantial leverage over a strategic national resource.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and fiscal vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic generation and a narrow revenue base leave Maseru dependent on external financing and regional power arrangements.

highlights: Ports and rail remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining concessions, especially around the Western Range, generate jobs and revenue but leave Liberia negotiating from a position of limited capital and infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Transport corridor control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors retain major influence over rail, port, and export logistics, limiting Liberia’s ability to capture full value from mineral production.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival authorities continue to contest budget allocations, export revenues, and influence over the National Oil Corporation, creating recurring risks of production disruption.

frictionVectors.title: External security patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian-linked, and other foreign security networks retain leverage through bases, contractors, and political partnerships tied to Libya’s strategic coastline and energy sector.

frictionVectors.title: Mining value-chain imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and related projects are dominated by foreign capital and technology, while Madagascar continues to struggle to secure greater local processing and fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and power dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak transport links increase reliance on external developers and lenders, reducing Antananarivo’s leverage in resource negotiations.

highlights: Mining expansion becomes a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining projects, including rare-earth and uranium prospects, offer badly needed foreign exchange but risk weak local value capture and limited fiscal transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on external lenders limit Malawi's bargaining power over transport, energy, and agricultural infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Gold wealth underwrites external security ties

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Cooperation with Russian-linked security actors has reduced Western leverage but raises concerns over opaque payment arrangements, mining access, and civilian protection.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking a larger share of industrial gold revenues, while insecurity, informal mining, and disputes with foreign operators continue to threaten production and sovereignty.

highlights: Iron and energy corridors remain externally financed

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen state revenues, but its cross-border structure and reliance on foreign operators limit near-term control over pricing, technology, and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and port infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital remains central to iron ore, green-hydrogen, rail, and port development, creating leverage risks even as Nouakchott diversifies partners.

highlights: Indian Ocean basing remains strategically sensitive

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago intersects with the future of the Diego Garcia military facility, placing strategic autonomy against major-power security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: External financial exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional capacity, but dependence on external finance, tourism, and global business services leaves it vulnerable to regulatory and geopolitical pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure projects in Western Sahara continue to generate legal and diplomatic friction over representation, consent, and external recognition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-funded connectivity
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and US investment in ports, rail, energy, and industrial zones expands Morocco's leverage but creates competing external interests around strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado and LNG Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity and dependence on foreign security forces continue to constrain sovereign control around the LNG projects. Any sustained deterioration could further delay investment and production.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mega-Projects
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, and Gulf-linked capital remains central to energy and infrastructure development, limiting domestic leverage over strategic assets and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Major Control of Offshore Oil
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries could transform state revenues, but international oil companies currently control much of the capital, technology, and operational capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Grid Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen projects face scarce water, limited transmission capacity, and competition over land and port infrastructure. Execution risks could shift benefits toward foreign developers.

frictionVectors.title: Benin Oil Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Benin threaten Niger's access to its main crude export route, exposing the limits of landlocked resource sovereignty and regional interdependence.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence and Mining Disruption
frictionVectors.details: The junta's break with Western partners and turn toward alternative security providers has increased uncertainty around uranium, gold, and oil operations amid persistent militant threats.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and community conflict continue to reduce state capture of oil revenues despite improved security coordination and higher domestic refining capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western firms remain important to ports, rail, refining, and energy finance, creating bargaining asymmetries over strategic infrastructure and future cash flows.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda facilitates or benefits from mineral flows linked to eastern DRC armed groups continue to generate diplomatic pressure and threaten access to responsible-sourcing markets.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control over domestic assets but remains exposed to donor conditionality and external scrutiny of its regional military and commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe remains reliant on foreign firms and partners to finance offshore exploration, limiting near-term bargaining power. Unproven reserves and weak fiscal capacity constrain national leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Security
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and maritime insecurity challenge control over the country's large ocean territory. External naval and development partners provide useful support but also deepen dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Operator Leverage
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production offers Senegal greater fiscal room, but international operators and lenders retain substantial influence over technology, marketing, and project finance.

frictionVectors.title: Mauritania Gas Coordination
frictionVectors.details: The shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project requires sustained Senegal-Mauritania coordination over revenue, infrastructure, and maritime governance. Delays or disputes could weaken the country's effort to convert gas into domestic industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on partners including India, France, and other maritime actors for surveillance, patrol capacity, and infrastructure. This supports sovereignty against illegal fishing while exposing the archipelago to wider strategic competition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Climate Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt-management and blue-finance initiatives have improved policy space, but tourism concentration and climate vulnerability leave critical infrastructure sensitive to external capital and shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects remain central to foreign exchange earnings, giving international firms significant influence over logistics, pricing, and fiscal outcomes. Weak local processing limits domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Finance Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external financiers remain important to roads, ports, and energy projects. Large infrastructure needs can narrow negotiating space when debt service, concession terms, and strategic access are linked.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Architecture
frictionVectors.details: Somalia's security and state-building remain heavily dependent on foreign military, financial, and diplomatic support. This assistance is essential against al-Shabaab but limits autonomous control over national security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and neighboring countries compete for influence over ports, maritime access, and infrastructure, while disputes involving Somaliland complicate federal claims to territorial sovereignty. Commercial and security agreements can outpace transparent national oversight.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND RAIL CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and freight-rail degradation continue to limit domestic control over mineral value chains and encourage private or foreign logistics alternatives.

frictionVectors.title: MINING INVESTMENT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater local processing and beneficiation, but dependence on external capital and technology complicates efforts to retain more value from platinum-group, manganese, and battery minerals.

frictionVectors.title: OIL EXPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Nearly total reliance on oil revenue leaves Juba vulnerable to pipeline disruptions, Sudanese transit politics, and the bargaining power of foreign operators and creditors.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND SECURITY EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Conflict risks and weak infrastructure make access to Sudanese and East African trade routes a major sovereignty constraint, while neighboring states retain substantial leverage over imports and exports.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks exploit gold and other revenues to sustain the conflict, reducing the authority of civilian institutions and enabling external buyers and sponsors to shape production flows.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, border routes, and agricultural zones is contested amid foreign diplomatic, military, and commercial involvement, leaving strategic infrastructure vulnerable to fragmentation.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for greater state participation, local processing, and revenue capture, but large-scale projects still depend on foreign finance, expertise, and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors increases strategic autonomy while drawing competition among Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional investors over infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND EXTERNAL CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a regional transshipment and commercial hub strengthens Togo's leverage, but port finance, logistics, and trade networks remain exposed to foreign operators and geopolitical competition.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel threatens transport and agricultural zones in northern Togo, increasing reliance on external security cooperation and constraining state control over border corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains financially constrained, increasing its dependence on European support and giving external partners leverage over migration enforcement and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: High reliance on imported hydrocarbons leaves Tunisia vulnerable to price shocks and limits strategic autonomy, despite renewable-energy potential and domestic phosphate resources.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline is strengthening Uganda's future export capacity while intensifying disputes over financing, environmental impacts, land acquisition, and dependence on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand Uganda's infrastructure base, but debt obligations and contractor dependence complicate efforts to retain full control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using global demand for copper and cobalt to seek better processing, tax, and local-content terms, while Chinese, Gulf, American, and European actors compete for influence.

frictionVectors.title: Power Shortages Constrain Mining Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Low hydropower output and grid fragility threaten mining expansion and increase reliance on imported electricity, emergency generation, and external infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-led investment dominates major lithium and other mineral projects, providing capital and market access but limiting Zimbabwe's leverage over processing, pricing, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted financing, and currency instability push Harare toward alternative partners while raising transaction costs and weakening transparent oversight of resource revenues.
